opus-5.5.text:
I think you really need both, and in a way they feed into each other. With the recurrent-depth model, the whole point was to see whether a model can do more computation in latent space, just by iterating a block more times at test time, rather than verbalizing everything as chain-of-thought tokens. So the first question was simply whether this works at scale. Can we train it stably, and does performance actually improve when you give it more recurrence? That's a capability question, and you have to answer it first, because if the thing doesn't work there's not much to understand.

But once it does work, the interesting part is what's happening inside those iterations. We saw some fun things when we looked at the latent trajectories: some tokens converge to a fixed point quickly, others seem to orbit, and for some, like numbers in arithmetic, you get these more structured, almost rotational patterns. That tells you the model isn't just doing the same thing as a deeper feedforward network. It's learned to use the recurrence in its own ways, and we didn't design that.

That's also why I think the understanding part matters so much here. One concern with latent reasoning is that you lose the readable chain of thought, which people like as a window into what the model is doing, even if that window isn't always faithful. If we move reasoning into continuous space, we owe the community better tools to inspect it. On the other hand, a recurrent model has some nice properties for analysis: it's the same weights applied repeatedly, so you can watch a computation unfold step by step and ask when it converges and why.

So in practice I'd say: push capabilities far enough to know the approach is real, then spend serious effort on analysis, and let what you learn guide the next round of design. Understanding convergence behavior, for example, directly gives you adaptive compute, letting the model stop early on easy tokens. That's a case where understanding the model immediately made it more useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses increasing recurrence at test time and balancing capability work with analysis, but it does not propose using more reasoning steps during cooldown than during pretraining.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because with latent reasoning you're kind of giving up something on purpose. With chain-of-thought models, the reasoning is right there in tokens, you can read it, and even if it's not perfectly faithful to what the model actually computed, you at least have a handle on it. When you move the reasoning into the latent space, where the model is iterating a recurrent block many times before it ever emits a token, you lose that readable trace. So the interpretability concern is real, and I don't want to wave it away.

That said, I'd push back a little on the framing that these are two competing goals you have to trade off. In our case I think they're actually pretty entangled. The recurrent-depth architecture is interesting precisely because it's a mechanism you can study. You have one block being applied over and over, you can look at the state after every iteration, you can watch how it converges, you can ask whether it's spinning in place or actually making progress on the problem. We saw things like the latent state orbiting or oscillating for certain kinds of tokens, numerical reasoning in particular, and that's the sort of behavior you simply wouldn't notice if you only looked at outputs. So in a weird way, the fact that the computation is explicit and repeated makes some kinds of analysis easier, not harder, even though the content of the computation isn't in natural language.

So my honest answer on balance is: at this stage, I think the capabilities work has to lead, but only slightly, and only because we don't yet know what these models are actually good at. If you build a small model that does recurrent latent reasoning and it just doesn't scale, then understanding it very deeply is a bit of an academic exercise. We need to know whether the approach is viable first. But the understanding work shouldn't be tacked on after the fact. We should be building these models from the start with the question in mind of how we are going to probe this, and the recurrent structure gives you a natural place to put those probes.

The other thing I'd say is that I'm a bit skeptical of the argument that we should avoid latent reasoning entirely because text-based reasoning is more legible. Partly because I'm not convinced the text trace is as trustworthy as people assume, and partly because if latent reasoning turns out to be substantially more efficient, people will build it anyway. So I'd rather we do this in the open, with small models, where we can actually develop the tools to look inside, than have it show up later in a frontier system that nobody can inspect.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses recurrent latent reasoning and probing its iterations, but does not propose using more reasoning steps during cooldown than during pretraining.

astra-6.text:
I think those two things should happen together. You want to push the model far enough that there’s something interesting to understand, but you also want experiments where you can tell why a change helped. If we just increase the amount of latent computation and get a better answer, that’s encouraging, but it doesn’t tell us what the model is doing with that computation.

So I’d want to look at both performance and the process: Does additional computation help on harder problems? Does the internal state keep changing in a meaningful way? And can we intervene in that process to test whether our explanation is actually correct?

There’s also a distinction between calling something reasoning and showing that it behaves like reasoning. I think we should be careful there. Developing the capabilities gives us phenomena to study, and understanding those phenomena should guide what we build next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those two things should go hand in hand. If we improve the model’s performance, we also want to understand what the additional computation is doing. Is it refining a useful representation? Is it correcting an earlier mistake? Or are we getting a benefit for some other reason?

With latent reasoning, that’s particularly interesting because we don’t have a sequence of words that we can read as an explanation. But a readable sequence wouldn’t, by itself, establish how the model works either. We need experiments where we intervene on the computation, change how long it runs, and examine when that helps and when it fails.

So I wouldn’t wait until we have the strongest possible model to start asking those questions. Understanding the mechanism can help us develop better capabilities, and it can tell us where our claims about reasoning are getting ahead of the evidence.

r001.rationale: The response advocates studying model behavior alongside capability improvements, but does not propose using more reasoning steps during cooldown than during pretraining.
